before: Naphtali; and for the tribe of Dan, the Amorites; and the tribe of Issachar; and for the tribe of Asher, the Perizzites (Joshua 19:25-26). Having distributed all this land, Jesus, having lived seventy and ten years, died (Joshua 24:20). And after the death of Eleazar the son of Aaron, Phinehas his son took up the high priesthood (Numbers 20:28).

But after the death of Joshua, the Israelites, having turned away from God, worshipped Astarte (Judges 2:11), and God delivered them into the hands of Cusharthan the Syrian king, who put them into much distress, so that, having been much afflicted, they cried out to God, and judges were given to them (Judges 2:11-16).

before: God having sent him, Moses, listening to His voice, declared the name of God to him; and Pharaoh, not having endured the hearing, fell speechless upon the earth. Moses, having approached, raised him up, and having engraved the holy name upon a tablet, sealed it; and one of the priests among the Egyptians, having dared to mock this name, immediately lost his life by a seizure. Pharaoh permitted Moses to perform some sign; and Moses, releasing the rod which he held, cast it upon the ground and changed it into a serpent; and he grasped it again and restored it to its former state.

But after this, when he would not release the people, Moses having prayed to God, a great earthquake accompanied by hail descended, so that those fleeing from the rooms were destroyed by the earthquake from the hail, and those hastening to turn away from the hail again were destroyed by the earthquake. And as he remained unmoved even after this, Moses struck the water of the Nile with the rod, and the river, having flooded Egypt, washed away all things to a very small degree, just as it has been done from that time until now, causing its descent. For Pharaoh, having summoned the priests over Memphis, threatened to destroy them and all those of the idols by fire, unless they performed wonders in the likeness of Moses.

But they, using customary sorceries, made a dragon emerge and discolored the river, intending that, through this being made murky, they might subject the Jews to the greatest punishment through Pharaoh. And Moses, striking the earth with the rod, prepared a certain flying creature to emerge from it, which, by clinging to the bodies, caused painful swellings to the Egyptians, so that they would be unable to provide any medical assistance to these. And as Pharaoh was hardened even by this scourge, he finally subjected all the firstborn of all Egypt to death. And when Egypt had been seized by immeasurable grief, Pharaoh expelled all the Jews from the land entirely; and having traveled a great way on this road, and having crossed the rivers of Arabia, they reached the Red Sea.

Because God hardened the heart of Pharaoh, the Egyptians, seized by the previous evils, pursued the Israelites along with Pharaoh. No one should suppose that Pharaoh was driven by God into insensitivity toward the things being done by force; for such a thing is perhaps judged as an injustice of God, with the one saying: 'If He himself hardens the heart, why is He blamed by the one being hardened?' But let it be known that the endurance of the whips was the cause of the hardening that happened to him; for whenever the plagues came upon him, he promised to release the people; but whenever he released him from the torments, he was being hardened. This is also signified by the word, and the Scripture says: 'And when Pharaoh saw that there was respite, he hardened his heart, and did not listen to them, just as the Lord spoke' (Exodus 10:20); and, 'For this very purpose I raised you up, so that I might show all my power to you' (Exodus 9:16).

But hearing this, do not suppose wrongly, saying: 'Why is He punishing them, while preparing him to oppose Him?' or 'Why does He strike, if there is no injustice on the part of God?' But let it be known first that things appearing to be contradictory to the Scripture are resolved not by reasoning, but by examples. For just as the best of physicians, striving to devise something useful for human nature, request to perform amputations on those subjected to fatal decisions, so that through those condemned to death they might bring something useful to men; so also God, surpassing all human wisdom, shows great signs through the unyielding Pharaoh who had sinned, punishing the one worthy of punishment, but healing those coming after this, providing for them the hypothesis of salvation through his own punishment.

Having gathered all his power, Pharaoh pursued the Israelites with two hundred chariots and myriads of horsemen. But those [Israelites], the Red Sea having been divided by Moses, were traveling by the command of God; and the Egyptians, driving after them, were crushed when Moses struck the staff and gathered the waters. On the next day, the weapons of the Egyptians were brought to the Hebrews by the water being pushed by the wind. And Moses, perceiving that even this was the providence of God, commanded them to gather them, so that they would not be without weapons. They arrive, indeed, into the wilderness. And Raguel and Jethro (for he happened to be of the same name) arrive to Moses, bringing to him...

before: After a time, He brings forth the Christ according to the flesh. And when the Magi from the East had worshiped Him as a king with gifts, Herod was troubled, and he was considering killing Him immediately. But He was carried away to Egypt by Joseph and Mary, and escaped death from Herod. Herod, being unaware of the flight, ordered all the children in Bethlehem to be killed; in which he even hurried to kill John while he was still an infant.

But Elizabeth, snatching him away, fled to the wilderness; and after her praying, the mountain was split, and she received the child, and the angel of God was guarding them. Then Herod sent to Zechariah: 'Give the son; tell me where you have hidden him.' But Zechariah replies to him, saying: 'I am always presiding at the altar; I do not know what happened to my son.' And Herod, having been angered, sent to him again, saying: 'Bring out your son. Do you not know that your blood is in my hand?' And Zechariah said: 'I am a witness of God. You have my blood, but God has my spirit. Receive and know that you are pouring out innocent blood at the thresholds of the temple of the Lord.'

And Herod, being angry at these things, ordered him to be killed in the midst of the altar before the dawning, so that his killing would not be hindered by the people. At dawn, the priests, having come to the temple, were astonished, according to the custom, not having met the high priest and remaining outside. When an hour had passed, one of them dared to enter. He sees congealed blood by the altar, and hears a voice saying: 'Zechariah has been murdered, and his blood shall not be wiped away until the avenger comes.' Hearing these things, he became terrified, and coming out, he reported to the priests.

They, having entered, saw not the body, except the blood, and having torn their robes, they cut themselves, and they announced to the people, and for three days and nights they made mourning over him. And after these things, they appointed Simeon to his rank by lot, who had been under the Holy Spirit, having been promised not to see death until he saw the Christ of the Lord.

Another story concerning Zacharias is brought forward: how there was a certain place near the temple where only virgins used to go out, entering to worship God, and those who were married were not permitted. Thus Mary, having given birth to the Savior, having come, stood in this place. Since those knowing that she had given birth were preventing her, Zacharias said that she was worthy of the place of virgins. Therefore, as they were committing him an error regarding the place of virgins, they killed him between the altar. And these things were said in passing.

But Joseph, having been sent to Egypt by the brothers, was established as ruler of all Egypt by a divine inspiration of the Pharaoh, discerning dreams. And as famine was pressing all the earth, his brothers went down to Egypt, buying grain themselves because of the famine; and Joseph, having been recognized by them, brought them together with their father Jacob into Egypt in their entirety (Gen 46:31).

To Reuben four children were born: Enoch, Phales, Arrom, Charmei; to Simeon six: Jebuel, Jabin, Aod, Achih, Sadhi, Saul; and to Levi three: Gedson, Boad, and Menare; and to Judah five: Er, Aunon, who, as was foretold (Gen 49:3-5), died, Shelom, Phares, Zara; and to Phares two: Arrom, and Jemoehl; and to Issachar four: Thala, Phona, Jasoph, Zabran; to Zebulun three: Serder, Aldon, Aiel; all thirty-three, having the lineage of Leah, and the daughter Dinah. And to Gad seven sons were born: Saphon, Anges, Saunis, Thasobath, Aedis, Anoedes, Ariles; to Asher four: Jemna, Iul, Meria, and Serathygaeter; and from Beriah were born Chobor and Melchiel; all these sixteen are the sons of Zelpah the handmaid, who bore them to Jacob in the name of Leah.

And to Joseph in Egypt two children were born: Manasseh and Ephraim, whom Aseneth, the daughter of Potiphera, the son of the Sun, bore to him. And from Manasseh was born Maher, of Syrian stock by lineage; and Maher begat Gilead; and from Ephraim were born the sons Sutalam, Bad, and Lam. And from Sutalam was born Eden. To Benjamin, two children were born: Ballachobor and Assaher; and from Ballachobor Geran, and Noemim, and Laches, and Esrom, and Mamphi. And Mamphi begat Arad; all these are the eighteen sons of Rachel. And to Dad a son was born; and to Naphtali Asiel, and Goumin, and Isaar.

before: the wife and the sons; and having learned all the wonder-working of God concerning the Egyptians from him, he was struck with amazement, and he glorified God. And this man, as they say, was a descendant of Abraham, born of one of those begotten to him from Hetur; for from Jezan came Dadan, Raguel, Jethor, and Obab. Therefore, Moses, having held him in high regard, sent him to his own homes. And Moses, having legislated many things for the benefit of the Hebrews, ended his life, having lived 120 years. And Joshua the son of Nun succeeds to his leadership, and leads the people out of the wilderness, having wandered in it for 40 years, upon which the traces of the habitation of the Jews are still preserved. For, thanks to the history, those arriving at the places report that the types of the tents still stand, existing in myriads, and that Mount Sinai is seen, at which Moses received the legislations, and each of those things written in detail.

The Hebrews sojourned in Egypt for 430 and 40 years, not 210 and 200; the record of the years is sufficient at 430, but the Scripture says 430 and 40. For it says, 'the seed of Abraham shall be a sojourner in a foreign land for 430 years' (Genesis 15:13). First, therefore, it must be noted that it did not say 'in Egypt,' but 'in a foreign land shall the seed of Abraham be a sojourner'; and a foreign land indeed existed, namely the Canaanite land, in which Isaac sojourned, the seed of Abraham himself being above all an exceptional one, for he was a son. It is therefore evident that before inheriting the land of the foreign tribes, they were sojourners for 430 years, just as the Apostle also says: 'a covenant having been proclaimed by God after 430 years, in order to bring forth the promise' (Galatians 3:17); and he adds: 'To Abraham, through a promise, God granted' (Genesis 12:7). It is therefore probable that they sojourned in Canaan for 430, and in Egypt for 430, which is the same as 430 years.

When Joshua led the people and the ark of the Covenant through the Jordan, the waters stood apart as a single heap, having stood far off; but that which was descending into the sea of the waves went down, until it vanished completely, and all crossed on dry land, and they are encamped at Jericho. And this [city] was fortified against the greatest with walls.

They circled it for six days by God's command; and on the seventh at dawn they circled it seven times, and the priests, having blown the trumpets, roused the people to shout together with a great cry; and as they helped, the wall fell immediately, and the city was captured, and all became a devoted thing to the Lord. Then Ai was besieged, and they took it and burned it, and having hung its king on a tree, they crucified him by the command of Joshua. And as the sun was setting, they threw his body into a ravine and covered it with a heap of stones.

But the Gibeonites, inquiring about these sieges (for they had spies), craftily deceived the Israelites. For if they had not reached their city first, they would have met them wearing worn-out clothes and sandals, having put on torn garments and sacks of dry bread and barley, and having put on old sacks, saying to them: 'Our city was greatly divided from us; for we prepared these fresh loaves, and the clothes we wear are new, and we gave new sandals to those walking; and all this the length of the road wore out and aged. Therefore make peace with us, and make our friends.' And the blessed Joshua pledged peace to them by oaths.

Later, having recognized their craftiness, he refrained from them because of the oath, but commanded that they should be beaten and carry water for the Israelites instead of the deceit. Then the king of Jerusalem, Adoni-Bezek, being angry at the Gibeonites acting alone, took allies from the nearby regions—the king of Hebron, Aila, the Fidon of Jerimuth, Ziphah of Lachish, and even Dad of Sodom—and marched against them and besieged Gibeon. The Gibeonites, being pursued, sent ambassadors to Joshua. He, being at Galgal, opposed them, and when battle occurred, the foreigners were routed; some were destroyed by the sword, others by hail. For as they fled, God rained hail upon them, which killed more of the adversaries than the war did. So that Joshua might completely destroy them, he prayed...
